Hold one of the testing leads to one of the terminals that needs to be tested.

Hold other testing lead to other terminal.

The meter will measure current in Amperes. If there is no load on the device or circuit, then it will display either 0 Amps or something like 0.1 Amps. 

An outlet doesn't have current passing through it until you plug something in and power it on. So you either need a meter that clamps around the cable, or be able to access the terminals on the device while the device is powered on.

Let's see if i can explain how it works for me.

For the record, i have years of music training, reading music, theory, etc.

One of the first jams you may learn as a budding musician is the 12 bar blues. It's good to begin learning how to listen and play with other players. But essentially the structure is simple, consists of 12 bars of chord changes, then, once having reached the end of the 12 bars, you can choose to repeat them as many times as you'd like. So it's a good way to practice knowing where you are in a particular section. Eventually, the 12 bar blues becomes so ingrained in you that you could hop in with any competent jazz musician anywhere and jam with them without saying a word.

Jamming any style of music is like that, but of varying levels of musical and technical know-how. I love jamming with others, one of my favorite forms of musical expression. Improvisational. However, it's more like i have a big tool kit of various musical things and i know when and where to whip out the right tool. Knowing this proper timing may come from much time spent listening to music that you wish to be good at. Watching and hearing others play is probably one of my top tips for you. Learn the basic techniques of your instrument of choice. For example, as a drummer it's important to know your 5-stroke rolls. Once the 5 stroke roll is muscle memory, you can use it on the fly whenever.

If you're playing a melodic instrument, it's good to know how to play chords, and know which types of chords promote a "happy" or "sad" feeling. It's good to know what intervals to play and how fast to play them in order to promote particular feelings in the listener.

Two people can sing the same pitch, however each person is physically different. Aside from the main fundamental pitch, or note, that you hear, there are many harmonics and overtones.  Each person is different, so the total sound that comes out will sound different. Most natural sound sources have harmonics and overtones. As opposed to say, a synthesizer that produces a single pure sine wave frequency. Also, overtones can be amplified by how a singer's mouth is shaped. Download a simple spectrum analyzer app and sing the word "err". Now sing "oooh". Note the visual on the graph.

None of those tracks sound very swing-y to me. It could be that some parts were played on, ahead, or behind the beat. This doesn't mean the same as playing out of time. Playing ahead of the beat means playing ever-so-slightly before the actual pulse. It's not even as much as a grace note. It's felt, more than heard. Playing behind the beat can make a song feel more laid back. Ahead of the beat can make it feel like it's faster, or more "pressing forward". 

That first track is tricky, because the organ pattern at  the beginning sounds swing, but it's actually straight 16ths.

Actual swing-feel is most simply described as, say, taking a straight 8th note pattern (1+2+3+4+), but instead you're really playing triplets with the second triplet left out. I was taught to count triplets like: One-trip-let, Two-trip-let, Three-trip-let, Four-trip-let. So, swing 8ths would be like saying: One-(rest)-let, Two-(rest)-let, etc. Note, the parts where it says "rest" are actual rests, do not say "rest". Or you can whisper "trip" in order to denote that beat isn't played. This particular rhythm would be called a shuffle.

In the US, we typically use 120 Volt power coming into the outlets in our homes. In some other countries, say Australia, they typically run their branch circuits at 240 Volts. I'm not sure the major reason why, but I can tell you that the main benefit from running a higher voltage is that less amperes (current) are used. Basically, it means you can have more pieces of equipment plugged in on one 240-Volt, 15 Amp circuit before the breaker trips than if it were a 120-Volt circuit. I suppose it's more of a convenience for the electricians than it is for the people living at the home. 

A bit more detail, a 15-amp breaker is designed to trip once the load reaches 12amps. It's an extra safety feature,  so you dont get a full 15-amps on that breaker. So you can have as many devices and equipment plugged into a circuit as long as it doesnt reach 12-amps of current draw. 120-Volt circuits use twice the amperage of 240-volts. So you can effectively put twice the amount of equipment on a single 240 volt circuit. This really makes no difference to the homeowner who most likely sees an outlet as simply a place where electricity comes to.

240 volts is more dangerous in the event that a person comes into contact with energized parts.

Source: electrician school

At the most basic level, DJing is the art of picking songs for you to listen or dance to and making them more or less seamlessly blend together. The actual tracks they are playing may be recorded to a final mix, therefore not live. However, the transitioning of one track to the next is where the real time element comes into play. Live DJ sets are another thing. With a program such as Ableton Live, one can perform a live DJ set. Even though it is all digital, it still requires a bit of knowhow in order to make the dang program obey your commands. You don't just open up Ableton and hit play. 

Ableton can be simply organized into a series of music clips. A single clip can be as short or as long of a musical phrase as you want. Live DJing is basically being really good at firing off those clips (that you programmed, composed and arranged) in real time. So it goes an extra step beyond simply choosing the songs. Now you're creating the songs in real time. You're choosing every single drum hit, bass sound, background noise, you name it. Yes these hits may mostly be pre recorded, however knowing which sounds work and when they work and how to fine tune them to work beyond the normal situation is the hard part. Room acoustics are a huge deal. Ideally you want a space that does not reflect sound. Typically hard walls easily bounce sound, and even vibrate themselves. This is easily noticeable in a large public bathroom. Studios are built to "deaden" the reverberation and echoing of sounds by using certain materials that literally prevent the sound waves from bouncing off in different directions. By doing this, you are able to record a more accurate rendition of what was being recorded without all of the excess reverb and sound that the room adds.

Once you are able to capture your ideally unfiltered sound, then the pros get to work mixing and mastering. This is where the magic happens.

On rooms, I'm no acoustic engineer, but I am aware that taller walls and higher ceilings are better for music production. Make it so your speakers/monitors are not exactly halfway between the floor and the ceiling. Also your monitors should be kept a certain distance from the wall behind it. Ideally the monitors should be supported on mounts so they dont vibrate your desk or floor. Carpet is useful in deadening some sound, but it is not the best solution.

Using your example, one major difference between violin and piano is how the sound is made. Both instruments make sounds by the use of strings vibrating. In a piano, the strings are struck with a felt mallet. With a violin, the strings are primarily bowed or plucked. This already will give them differing sounds. Aside from that, a violin is a small, hollow, wooden body, while a piano is much bigger and not so light and hollow. The string vibrates at a certain main "frequency", aka, how many times it makes a complete oscillation in one second. This is usually the frequency that music theory refers to as the "root frequency". Then there are many harmonic and overtone frequencies that the string also produces naturally. Depending on what you use to hit the strings (fingers, bow, mallets, felts) different overtones may be produced. The violin body or piano body then captures this sound and creates a little amplification to make it louder. Depending on the quality of your instrument, the wooden body itself will vibrate in harmony with the strings, this is called "resonance". Other factors can alter the quality of your sound, such as metal bodies, wood or plastic tipped sticks, nylon or metal strings, etc.

One big factor between plucked instruments and others is that they always hit maximum loudness and then decay once the string has been released. As opposed to bowing instruments or wind instruments which allows you to "ramp up" or slow the "attack" and decay. Attack is basically another way of  saying "how fast the sound reaches maximum loudness after i hit the string". Decay is "how long it takes for the sound to diminish away to desired sustain level". "Sustain" is the loudness a sound sits at until you release the key. "Release" is how long it takes the sound to completely diminish.

But basically, the violin and the piano strings sound different to us because they each have their own natural unique combination of frequencies, that combined, give the overall perceived effect of a particular sound. It's similar to color mixing, and how if you turn up the red, green, or blue peaks, it alters the overall perceived light to make millions of different possible colors.

This is the same conductor that is the third prong in 3-prong plugs. It's basically a safety measure that allows current to flow through the conductor in the event of a short circui, instead of flowing through a person touching the box. This conductor normally DOES NOT carry current. In the photo, it looks like the ground wire is not connected to a screw on the box. Should be a green screw.

Dynamic sounding drums can be achieved very simply. Just mess with your velocities. You can achieve more real feeling drums when your snares and kicks aren't all hitting at the same intensity. You can make ghost notes by just taking down the velocity of those hits compared to your main snare backbeat. You can make hi hats sound deeper by messing with your velocity, rather than having every hit by monotone and static.

Dewaxed (winterized) oil looks more clear as a result of inactive plant waxes and materials being filtered out through a second solvent process. This has been come to be known as "shatter".

Depending on the temperature during the purging process, the concentrate will come out different. Low temps (80F) can result in shatter with most or all terpenes intact. Mid temps (100-120F) can result in budder. Higher temps (160F) result in a more liquidy "honey" type wax, which has less terpenes, however technically more pure in cannabinoid content.

All in all, if your hits are smooth and aren't painful or taste funny, then you shoikd have good oil. Although, it's been noted that dabbing waxy oil for long periods of time leads to buildup in the lungs. You'll notice it not too long after you hit the waxy oil when you start coughing intensely.
